summary: Wineberry is a shrub related to raspberries and blackberries that forms spiny, impenetrable thickets, lowering an area's value for wildlife and for people. It replaces native plants, including native berry bushes, and can spread even into mature forests. You can recognize it by its reddish stems, which are covered in dense red hairs, its leaves with three leaflets that are silvery underneath, and its bright red berries.
history: Wineberry is native to East Asia. It was brought to North America in the 1890s as breeding stock for raspberries, and by the 1970s it was found invading natural areas. It is now recorded in most states east of the Mississippi River.
seasons: Leaves come out in April and flowers in May, with fruit from late June to August; the leaves drop in late November. Each cane lives two years: it grows leaves in its first year, then flowers and fruits in its second. Its long canes can take root where their tips touch the ground.

handling.text: Wineberry is armed with thorns and hairs, so minimize exposed skin when handling it. It is easier to control than many invasive plants because it lacks a strong underground root system: small patches can be hand-pulled or dug out, with follow-up visits for a few years to remove new plants sprouting from root pieces. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
